description: Compare the best RO water purifiers in India by TDS handling, recovery rate, storage tank, and after-sales service — so you can pick the right one for hard water, borewell, or municipal supply.

headings.text: What actually matters in an RO water purifier in 2026

cta.headline: Hard water ruining your geyser and washing machine?
cta.sub: Our hard-water guide covers descaling, sediment filters, and water-softener upgrades that protect your appliances.

tldr_pick: The Kent Grand Plus (11016) is the best RO water purifier in India for most homes in 2026: a 9 L tank, 75% recovery rate, UV+UF post-treatment, and a service network that actually answers the phone in tier-1 and tier-2 cities.
key_takeaways: Recovery rate matters more than litre capacity — a 75% recovery RO wastes 1 L per 4 L purified; a 50% recovery RO wastes 1 L per 2 L.
UV after RO only matters for municipal supply — borewell water with TDS under 2000 doesn't need UV, and adding it just adds cost.
TDS controller is non-negotiable above 500 ppm input — without it, RO water tastes flat and pulls minerals out of food and tea.
Service network beats specifications on paper — a Kent / Pureit / Aquaguard with average specs and 90-minute city SLA beats a brand with great specs and 5-day callbacks.
who_for: Indian households on municipal, borewell, or tanker supply that need an RO + UV purifier with a credible service network and 8–12 L of storage. Not aimed at commercial kitchens or industrial TDS levels.
methodology: We compared 8 popular RO water purifiers sold in India in 2026 against the three most common input-water scenarios: municipal supply (TDS 200–500), borewell (TDS 500–1500), and tanker / mixed supply (TDS variable). Recovery rate, storage, post-treatment, and service-network reach were weighted equally. Pricing is the current normal sale price on Amazon India and Flipkart; verify the exact model code on the listing before purchase.

faq.q: Do I actually need an RO water purifier in India?
faq.a: It depends on your input water. If your municipal supply or borewell has TDS above 500 ppm (most of India does), RO is the practical choice. Below 300 ppm, a UV-only purifier works and keeps minerals in the water. RO strips out everything — including the minerals that make water taste good — which is why TDS controllers and copper / mineral cartridges exist.

faq.q: What is the recovery rate and why does it matter?
faq.a: Recovery rate is the percentage of input water that becomes purified water. A 75% recovery RO turns 4 L of input into 3 L of purified water and wastes 1 L. A 50% recovery RO turns 4 L into 2 L and wastes 2 L. In water-scarce cities — Chennai, Bengaluru, parts of Mumbai — the higher recovery rate is worth a small premium. In areas with cheap piped water, the recovery rate is mostly a billing question.

faq.q: How often do I need to change the filters?
faq.a: For a typical Indian household (20–30 L/day), the sediment and carbon pre-filters need changing every 6 months, the RO membrane every 12–18 months, and the UV lamp every 12 months. The TDS controller and post-carbon filter usually run 12–18 months. Most brands offer annual maintenance contracts (AMC) at ₹1,500–₹3,000 that cover all of this plus a free service visit.

faq.q: Is the storage tank of 7–9 L really enough?
faq.a: For a family of 4–5, 8 L is the practical minimum. RO purifiers produce water slowly — usually 8–15 L per hour — so the tank is what you drink from during the day. Purely tankless RO units exist (they connect directly to a tap) but they have a much lower flow rate and aren't practical for Indian cooking volumes. If you have a large family or cook a lot of dal and rice, go for 9 L or larger.

faq.q: Can I install an RO purifier myself?
faq.a: Technically yes, but most brands require authorised installation for the warranty to hold. The install takes 30–60 minutes and typically involves a water-supply tap connector, a drain line, and a wall mount. The first service visit is usually free with a new purchase; the AMC kicks in from year 2.
